quote: Ist die Reihe der merkwürdigen Punkte des Pascal- schen Sechsecks: Pascal, Steiner, Cirquemann' sche Punkte, ins unendliche fortzusetzen
english: Can the series of notable points of the Pascal hexagon (Pascal, Steiner, Kirkman points) be continued to infinity?
topic: A list of research problems and plans: shortening Kummer's proof in cyclotomic fields, extending the Pascal hexagon's notable points, Euler's Diophantine problem, division of the lemniscate arc into a+ib parts, transferring Staude's string construction of the ellipsoid, and treating the fields √(a+bi) and ∛α to derive reciprocity laws.

triage.modern_statement: Take six points on a nonsingular conic. Ordering them in different ways gives 60 hexagons, and Pascal's theorem gives each one a Pascal line. These lines satisfy concurrence theorems that produce new points: 20 Steiner points and 60 Kirkman points. The new points satisfy collinearity theorems that produce more lines (Cayley–Salmon, Plücker), and these in turn produce more points (Salmon points). Hilbert asks whether this alternation of incidence theorems keeps going forever, giving infinitely many 'notable' points and lines, or whether the 'hexagrammum mysticum' closes up after finitely many steps.
triage.answered_by: Mainly Giuseppe Veronese, 'Nuovi teoremi sull'hexagrammum mysticum' (1877). This probably predates Hilbert's note. He went past the classical 95 points and 95 lines by building a 'multimysticum' of 'higher' Pascal lines and meeting points. The Illumination paper (arXiv 1209.4795) says someone proved there are infinitely many systems of sixty lines and points. The snippet I saw does not name that person; it is probably Veronese, but I did not confirm this. In the same period Cremona tied the configuration to cubic surfaces. Modern work: Conway & Ryba, 'Extending the Pascal Mysticum', Math. Intelligencer 35 (2013), 44–51, and Chipalkatti's papers on Veronese's construction (arXiv 2007.04315 and others). I found no source that addresses Hilbert's question directly.

evidence.claim: The classical hexagrammum mysticum has 95 points (60 Kirkman, 20 Steiner, 15 Salmon) and 95 lines (60 Pascal, 20 Cayley, 15 Plücker).

Conway and Ryba (The Pascal Mysticum Demystified) write that Veronese drops the requirement that the three points or lines be named after the same mathematician and finds 'higher' Pascal lines. They also note that Cremona got the same results from the cubic-surface configuration.

Chipalkatti's paper describes the Pascal lines satisfying concurrence theorems that give new points, which then satisfy collinearity theorems, 'eventually leading to' a very large structure. In Veronese's 1877 multimysticum, linking lines and higher meeting points connect successive stages.
A 2012 paper reviewing the history says it was proved that there are infinitely many systems consisting of sixty lines and points. The snippet I saw does not show who proved it.
Conway & Ryba published 'Extending the Pascal Mysticum' in The Mathematical Intelligencer 35 (2013), pp. 44–51.

Recent research on the configuration: Chipalkatti, 'The conjugacy locus of Cayley–Salmon lines' (Adv. Geom. 2018), 'Pascal's Hexagram and Desargues Configurations' (Math. Pannonica 2021), and 'Degenerations of Pascal Lines' (2022).

triage.why: The question is a real research question about extending the hexagrammum mysticum. It is not among Hilbert's 23 problems or the 24th problem. Veronese (1877) and Cremona had already gone well beyond the Pascal/Steiner/Kirkman level. Veronese built higher Pascal lines and points in a multimysticum. One source says it was proved that there are infinitely many systems of sixty lines and points, but the snippet does not say who proved it, so I cannot confirm it was Veronese. That supports a positive answer to 'can it be continued?', although the sources I saw do not say exactly in what sense. Conway–Ryba (2013) and Chipalkatti (2016–2022) continue this work, so the area is still active in a small classical-geometry niche. My search budget ran out before I could read Veronese's exact statement or the full Conway–Ryba text, so this conclusion is medium confidence and not a confirmed 'solved'.
